## Plain-text file formats {#plain-text-is-the-format-that-survives}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/terminal.png" alt="R script"><span class="name">.R</span><span class="what">Code only, with prose in comments.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/markdown.png" alt="Markdown"><span class="name">.md</span><span class="what">Prose only: headings, lists, links, and no code.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/rmarkdown.png" alt="R Markdown"><span class="name">.Rmd</span><span class="what">Prose and R, rendered together. R only.</span></div>
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/quarto.png" alt="Quarto"><span class="name">.qmd</span><span class="what">Prose and R, Python or Julia. The workshop's format.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small .fs-80}
Every one of these is a **plain text file**. You can open it in anything, compare two versions of it line by line, email it, and read it in twenty years. A `.docx` with pasted output is not plain text, and nothing in it records which numbers came from which code.
:::

::: notes
Here are four file types, in increasing order of what they hold. A dot R file is code with comments, a Markdown file is prose with no code, an R Markdown file is prose and R together, rendered into one document, and a Quarto file is the same idea, except that the code can be R, Python or Julia. Each of them is a plain text file, which you can open in any editor, compare line by line with an earlier version, email, and still read in twenty years. [advance] A Word document holding numbers pasted in from somewhere looks the same on the page, but nothing in it records which number came from which line of code, which is how the old value of a recomputed number can still be sitting in the paper.
:::
